summary: This note is a Monash University research-portal record for a 1995 Neuron article by Greg Stuart and Bert Sakmann on how synaptic potentials (EPSPs) are amplified by sodium channels in neocortical layer V pyramidal neurons. Using simultaneous somatic and dendritic recordings with simulated EPSPs, the authors found that sodium channels near the soma and in the axon amplify EPSPs, while calcium channel blockers had little effect. The page also includes citation formats and sharing links, which are boilerplate.
one_line: A 1995 Neuron article by Stuart and Sakmann showing that axosomatic sodium channels amplify EPSPs in neocortical pyramidal neurons.
key_facts: The article 'Amplification of EPSPs by axosomatic sodium channels in neocortical pyramidal neurons' was written by Greg Stuart and Bert Sakmann and published in Neuron in November 1995.
The article appears in Neuron volume 15, issue 5, pages 1065-1076.
The study made simultaneous somatic and dendritic recordings from the same neocortical layer V pyramidal neuron.
Current injection via the dendritic recording pipette was used to simulate the voltage change that occurs during an EPSP.
At the soma, simulated EPSPs increased nonlinearly with the amplitude of the dendritic current injection and with depolarization of the membrane potential.
Bath application of the sodium channel blocker TTX decreased large (>5 mV) EPSPs.
Bath application of TTX also blocked amplification of EPSPs at depolarized membrane potentials.
Calcium channel blockers had little effect on EPSP amplification.
Local application of TTX to the soma and axon blocked EPSP amplification, whereas dendritic application had little effect.
Simultaneous somatic and axonal recordings demonstrated that EPSP amplification was largest in the axon.
The authors conclude that EPSPs are amplified by voltage-activated sodium channels located close to the soma and in the axon.
The article had 353 citations in Scopus at the time of the record.
The article's DOI is 10.1016/0896-6273(95)90095-0 and it was published by Cell Press.
The acknowledgements thank Michael Häusser, Guy Major, Jackie and Izik Schiller, and Nelson Spruston, and note financial support from the Alexander von Humboldt Stiftung to G. S.
